Your letter received and on noticing the date I see that it has taken a month to arrive.

On your question as to how the war is progressing, I am afraid my answer is very different from what you will notice the difference between the reports of the Italian papers and those of the Germans: of course it is natural that each one should give as much credit to their country as possible.

And certainly would not be surprised if she did win. They were a good type, when they actually did make themselves and were not made by accidentally stubbing their toes on gold mines or oil wells. With all their faults one liked them better than some of their horrifying descendants. They were at least familiar with hard knocks. They had slept on hard beds or on no beds at all; they had undergone the hardship of dressing without a valet or walking without a cane; and they had known what it was to work until they were blind with weariness. The qualities by which they rose were not always admirable, but at least they were their own qualities, not those of an ancestor.

For the perpetuation of economic institutions the self-made man was a boon. He gave a fictitious interest to life in the United States. He proved that there were winning numbers on the wheel of fortune. The average man's chances, then as always, were slim; the bet against the average man was a hundred to one or worse. But the average man persuaded himself that he might be the lucky holder of the hundredth number in the lottery. He wanted no changes in the rules.

But those days waned in a second generation. They waned when the Morgans, Astors, Rockefellers, and hundreds of lesser beings the country over began to bequeath their fortunes and their power to heirs who had nothing to do with making the fortunes or assuming the power.
